**Diagnosis and Management of Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Narrative Review**

**Introduction and Classification**
Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is a progressive and historically underdiagnosed infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by the extracellular deposition of insoluble, misfolded amyloid fibrils within the myocardial interstitium [1]. This abnormal protein accumulation disrupts cardiac architecture, leading to restrictive filling, progressive heart failure, and life-threatening conduction disturbances [2]. While numerous precursor proteins can form amyloid, more than 95% of clinical CA cases stem from two primary types: light-chain (AL) amyloidosis and transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis [3]. AL amyloidosis is an acquired, hematologic disorder driven by a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia producing unstable monoclonal light chains [3]. Conversely, ATTR amyloidosis involves the destabilization of the transport protein transthyretin, which is synthesized predominantly in the liver [1]. ATTR is further subclassified into wild-type ATTR (ATTRwt), an age-related systemic condition, and hereditary or variant ATTR (ATTRv), which is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with variable penetrance [4].

**Clinical Presentation and Diagnostic Red Flags**
The clinical hallmark of CA is a restrictive cardiomyopathy, typically manifesting as heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [5]. Common symptoms include exertional dyspnea, fatigue, lower extremity edema, and angina [6]. Several extracardiac "red flags" are crucial to prompt early diagnostic evaluation, such as bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, spontaneous biceps tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, and orthostatic hypotension [1]. Standard diagnostic clues include low QRS voltage on electrocardiography (ECG)—which contrasts sharply with the marked ventricular thickening seen on imaging—or a pseudo-infarction pattern [7]. Echocardiography classically reveals symmetric concentric ventricular wall thickening, a restrictive filling pattern, and a highly specific "apical sparing" pattern on global longitudinal strain analysis [8]. Proper classification according to international nomenclature guidelines is vital to direct treatment [9].

**Diagnostic Pathway and Non-Biopsy Diagnosis**
Differentiating between AL and ATTR CA is a clinical emergency, as treatment pathways diverge entirely [3]. A landmark multicenter study established a highly accurate, non-invasive diagnostic algorithm for ATTR CA [10]. The first step in this algorithm is screening for a monoclonal gammopathy using a combination of serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis alongside a serum free light chain (FLC) assay [10]. If a monoclonal protein is ruled out, a definitive diagnosis of ATTR CA can be made non-invasively through bone scintigraphy (using $^{99\text{m}}\text{Tc}$-pyrophosphate or $^{99\text{m}}\text{Tc}$-3,3-diphosphono-1,2-propanodicarboxylic acid) showing Grade 2 or 3 myocardial radiotracer uptake [10,11]. However, if a monoclonal protein is detected, histological confirmation via tissue biopsy remains mandatory to rule out AL amyloidosis [10]. Subtyping of biopsy specimens is historically performed using immunohistochemistry, but laser microdissection with tandem mass spectrometry (LMD-MS) has emerged as the gold standard for high-specificity typing [12].

Multimodality imaging has also advanced considerably [13]. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging is highly sensitive, demonstrating diffuse, subendocardial, or transmural late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) [14] and permitting the quantification of extracellular volume (ECV) fraction [14]. These CMR parameters are robust markers of disease severity and correlate strongly with adverse clinical outcomes [15]. Prognostic risk-stratification for AL amyloidosis relies on staging systems utilizing cardiac troponins and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) [16,17], whereas ATTR staging utilizes NT-proBNP and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) [18,19].

**Therapeutic Breakthroughs**
Therapy in CA targets both symptom management and etiologic-specific pathways [3]. 

*AL Amyloidosis*:
The therapeutic goal in AL CA is rapid elimination of the hematologic clone to halt light chain production [20]. The landmark ANDROMEDA trial redefined the standard of care, showing that adding the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody daratumumab to cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone (CyBorD) yielded superior hematologic complete responses and significantly improved organ-progression-free survival [21,22].

*ATTR Amyloidosis*:
For ATTR CA, therapies either stabilize the circulating TTR tetramer or silence hepatic TTR production [23]. The Phase 3 ATTR-ACT trial demonstrated that the TTR stabilizer tafamidis significantly reduced all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations in both ATTRwt and ATTRv patients [24]. More recently, the high-affinity stabilizer acoramidis achieved robust tetramer stabilization and significant clinical outcomes in the ATTRibute-CM trial [25].

Hepatic TTR gene silencers use RNA interference (RNAi) or antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) to halt TTR production [26]. Patisiran, an RNAi therapeutic first approved for ATTRv polyneuropathy [26], demonstrated improvements in functional capacity and quality-of-life parameters in patients with ATTR-CM in the APOLLO-B trial [27]. Vutrisiran, a next-generation subcutaneous RNAi agent, recently demonstrated a substantial reduction in the composite endpoint of all-cause mortality and recurrent cardiovascular events in the HELIOS-B trial, positioning TTR silencing as a frontline strategy [28]. For patients with mixed neuropathic and cardiopathic phenotypes, the ASO eplontersen [29] and the first-generation ASO inotersen [30] offer further therapeutic options.

**Conclusion**
The paradigm of cardiac amyloidosis has shifted from a fatal, late-stage diagnosis to a highly treatable cardiomyopathy. Implementing screening with FLC assays and bone scintigraphy allows for rapid non-invasive diagnosis. The integration of daratumumab-based induction for AL, along with highly effective stabilizers and gene silencers for ATTR, highlights the paramount importance of early detection to prevent irreversible myocardial damage.
